description: Wallach 90-essentials data foundation. Per-essential: Wallach's stated baseline target dose (from Let's Play Doctor baseline supplement table where given), short notes, and confidence on the target. Used by dashboard/dashboard.html for coverage computation and by the agent for protocol reasoning.
source_primary: Let's Play Doctor (LPD) baseline supplement table for adults; Rare Earths element entries; DDDL condition-specific protocols. Cross-referenced against TRANSCRIPTIONS.md 90-nutrients graphic (with Niobium correction + K-form flag applied).
notes: Wallach's 90-essentials list per his own framing is 60 + 16 + 12 + 3 = 91 (the 'D2 and D3 considered a single vitamin' note in his graphic reduces vitamins from 17 to 16, yielding 90).
Vitamin K canonically = Menaquinone (K2 family) per Rare Earths book. The 90-nutrients graphic mislabels as K (Phylloquinone = K1) — graphic error per TRANSCRIPTIONS.md correction.

Many trace minerals (especially rare earths) have NO Wallach-specified individual dose. His framework treats them as 'covered by plant-derived colloidal minerals (humic shale)' as a group. Such minerals show wallach_baseline_target='trace via PDM'.
wallach_baseline_target uses the units specified in Wallach's LPD baseline supplement table where present. 'Unknown' means not given in the corpus locations searched.

Calcium is an essential 'macro' mineral, meaning we need large amounts in our daily diet to meet our metabolic needs. Calcium is required to maintain bone density, proper neuromuscular function, and blood clotting reactions.

Elevated calcium in blood is rare because of the 'homeostatic' mechanisms of the thyroid and parathyroid glands — when elevated calcium does occur, it signals major bone changes such as nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism (translates to overactive parathyroid glands from chronic calcium deficiency and/or phosphorus excess) or metastasis of cancer into bone.

Low blood calcium causes muscle spasms, tetany, cardiac arrhythmia, depression, and the classic Trousseau and Chvostek signs. Wallach's framework treats calcium as the load-bearing mineral for the entire skeletal system — bone is the body's calcium bank, and chronic depletion withdraws from that bank to maintain blood levels, causing osteoporosis decades later. Supplementation is upstream prevention; bone loss after menopause is downstream consequence.

wallach_stance.summary: Copper is essential to all living organisms and is a universally important cofactor for many hundreds of metalloenzymes. Copper is required for RNA and DNA, melanin production (hair and skin pigment), electron transfer of oxygen in subcellular respiration, and tensile strength of elastic fibers in blood vessels, skin, and vertebral discs.

wallach_stance.expanded_context:
Copper is essential to all living organisms and is a universally important cofactor for many hundreds of metalloenzymes. Copper deficiency is widespread and appears in many forms.

Copper is required in many physiological functions: RNA and DNA synthesis, lysil oxidase cofactor (the enzyme that cross-links collagen and elastin), melanin production for hair and skin pigment, electron transfer of oxygen in subcellular respiration, and tensile strength of elastic fibers in blood vessels, skin, and vertebral discs.

Neonatal enzootic ataxia (sway back) was recognized as a clinical entity in 1937 as a copper deficiency in pregnant sheep. Copper supplements prevented the syndrome, which was characterized by demyelination of the cerebellum and spinal cord — cavitation or gelatinous lesions of cerebral white matter, chromatolysis, nerve cell death, and myelin aplasia (failure to form).

The human equivalent shows up as gray hair, aneurysms (the tensile-strength failure), varicose veins, and Menkes' kinky hair syndrome. Wallach pairs copper with zinc in the supplementation framework — they compete for absorption, so isolated zinc supplementation can precipitate copper deficiency. The Healthy Body Start Pak delivers both at Wallach's chosen ratio rather than either alone.

Then there's those people who want to do things naturally. Let's see if you can do anything good with 10 lbs of spinach. And let's be fair, let's see if you can get 1,000 mg of magnesium.

I picked magnesium because in green leafy vegetables, you have a lot of magnesium because of the chlorophyll, right? It's part of the chlorophyll molecule. And any pound of anything, you got 454 g. In 10 lbs of spinach, you got 4,540 g, of which most of that, 97% is water. And let's say you have 1 g of chlorophyll in that 10 lbs of spinach, there's 50 mg of magnesium. You got to divide that into the thousand you want, you get a factor of 20, which you multiply times ten pounds. So you'd need 200 pounds of spinach every day to hit the magnesium target.

And we're just talking about magnesium. You've still got 59 more minerals to go, plus 16 vitamins, 12 amino acids, and 3 fatty acids. The math doesn't work — that's why supplementation isn't optional, it's structural.
